I’m currently pursuing a Master of Applied Economics and Data Science at the University of Pennsylvania. I have 4+ years of experience working in economic consulting supporting complex commercial litigation and international arbitration across Latin America and the U.S., with a focus on valuation, damages quantification, and IP/antitrust disputes.
My experience includes applying economic modeling, econometrics, event study analysis and financial analysis to matters involving claims from USD 2M to over USD 100M. I also have experience working across the full litigation lifecycle, including discovery, expert report preparation, deposition, and trial support.
Technical skills: Python, R, Stata, Excel.

title: Understanding the Welfare Cost of Business Cycles
text:
Recessions feel painful. People lose jobs, incomes shrink, families cut back on spending. So it seems that eliminating business cycles altogether would make society much better off. In 1987, economist Robert Lucas asked, if we could eliminate all the ups and downs in the economy (keeping only the long-run growth trend) how much would people be willing to pay for that?
The answer was surprising: almost nothing. According to Lucas’ calculations, the average American would trade less than half a percent of their consumption to eliminate every recession and boom forever. This is the welfare cost of business cycles, and its surprisingly small size became a famous results in macroeconomics.
The key insight is a distinction between the level of consumption and its variability. Business cycles don’t (in Lucas’s framework) change how much people consume on average. Instead they just make consumption bounce up and down around a stable trend. A recession is followed, on average, by a recovery.
People dislike risk, but they dislike it because of diminishing marginal utility. Losing \(1,000\) hurts more than gaining \(1,000\) helps. So variability around a fixed average is costly, but only mildly costly, because the swings that make up actual business cycles are small relative to how much income grows decade after decade. Compare a typical recession which might reduce consumption by 2–3% for a year or two with long-term economic growth that raises consumption by a considerably larger magnitude.
Economists measure how much a household would pay to avoid risk using utility functions like:
\[u(c)=\frac{c^{1-\sigma}-1}{1-\sigma}\] where \(\sigma\) measures the risk aversion (the higher \(\sigma\), the higher the aversion to risk).
If consumption fluctuates with variance \(\sigma^2_c\) around a mean of \(1\), a standard approximation shows that the cost of business cycles, which is denoted as \(g\) and can be thought of as the fraction of consumption a household would sacrifice to make consumption perfectly stable, is approximately:
\[g\approx \frac{1}{2}\sigma \sigma^2_c\] This formula carries the whole intuition. The cost scales with the variance of consumption, multiplied by how risk-averse people are. Since actual measured consumption volatility is small (\(\sigma^2_c\) is on the order of a few tenths of a percent), even with fairly high risk aversion, \(g\) comes out small (only a fraction of one percent).
Lucas’s 1987 calculation landed at a pivotal moment. Since Keynes, much of macroeconomics had been built around the premise that smoothing business cycles through fiscal and monetary policy was the central task of the discipline. Lucas’s result flipped the priority, because if fluctuations barely matter for welfare, then the big prize is economic growth, not stabilization.
The result may not appear intuitive at first. Recessions feel devastating, especially to people who lose jobs or homes. Lucas’s calculation, however, uses aggregate, average consumption, which is remarkably smooth even during recessions (most people keep their jobs and incomes even in bad years). But the pain of a recession is concentrated: unemployment, foreclosure, and bankruptcy hit a minority of households very hard, while the majority barely notice. Averaging across everyone hides this uneven distribution.
Given these considerations, there have been decades of follow-up research. This research suggests that incorporating uninsurable individual-level risk, unemployment spells, effects of recessions on long-run growth, and the asymmetric nature of downturns all push the estimated welfare cost higher.
As a result of these new observations, a more recent consensus on Lucas’s calculation is that, though not wrong, it could be narrow. Incorporating the idea that real business cycles are not necessarily smooth, symmetric, or evenly felt to Lucas’ estimation might shed new insights as to how households deal with economic downturns in a more precise way.

title: Are bigger cities more expensive?
text:
Source: Von Deensel - Puerto Madero, Buenos Aires, CC BY 2.0


Big cities are assumed to cost more to live in. Tokyo, Shanghai and Delhi, surely all that scale drives prices up? I decided to test that assumption directly, and the answer turned out to be more interesting than a simple yes or no.
To do this, I pulled population data for the world’s largest cities from Wikipedia, then matched each one against Numbeo’s crowdsourced cost-of-living rankings. Numbeo’s database scores cities on prices for groceries, rent, restaurants, and more, all benchmarked against New York City (set at 100). Not every huge city has enough Numbeo data to be scored, so I widened my search until I found 100 large cities with reliable data, reaching as far as the 174th-largest city in the world to fill that quota, out of 479 cities Numbeo tracks overall. Considering this, it is important to note that my sample skews toward cities that are well-documented online, which tends to mean wealthier and more internationally connected cities. A lot of very large but less-tracked cities (particularly across parts of Africa and South Asia) simply didn’t have enough data for me to include.
For each city, I calculated a “value score” or local purchasing power divided by cost of living. This can be thought of as how far does a typical local salary actually stretch against local prices. A score above 1 means wages outpace costs and below 1 means the opposite.
Population size told me almost nothing about cost of living
When I ran the numbers, I found essentially no relationship between how big a city is and how expensive it is (see Figure 1). This correlation came out to -0.09, which is about as close to “no pattern” as real-world data gets. Some of the cheapest cities I measured (several mid-sized Indian cities) sit right alongside some of the world’s largest metros in population, while a few smaller cities on my list were nearly as pricey as New York. The old assumption that scale drives up cost simply doesn’t hold once I looked past a handful of famous outliers like Tokyo or Shanghai.






Figure 1



India’s mid-size tech hubs offer exceptional value
The top of my best-value list was dominated by Indian cities: Hyderabad topped the list with a value score of 7.1, followed by Pune, Chennai, and Bangalore all above 5 (see Figure 2). That means a typical local salary in Hyderabad buys roughly seven times more relative to living costs than the same ratio in a low-value city like Addis Ababa. Two Chinese cities, Chongqing and Chengdu, are also in my top 10. The takeaway here is that, for remote workers with location flexibility, employers setting cost-of-living-adjusted salaries, or companies scouting new office locations, these cities represent a genuinely underrated combination of large talent pools and strong purchasing power. This does not mean that they are just “cheap,” but cheap relative to what people there actually earn.






Figure 2



“Worst value” hid two very different stories
My bottom 10 split into two distinct groups, and the difference matters a lot in practice. Mexico City, Tehran, Cairo, Buenos Aires, and New York City itself all scored close to 1.0, meaning costs and local purchasing power are roughly balanced there (see Figure 3). That’s not necessarily bad, it is just average.
The real outliers I found were Abidjan and Addis Ababa, scoring 0.28 and 0.27, considerably lower than everywhere else on the list. Here’s the nuance I want to highlight: these cities aren’t expensive by sticker price (their cost-of-living index is actually moderate). What drags their score down is very low local purchasing power. Wages are simply too low relative to even modest costs. This is a distinct problem from high prices, and it might call for a different response. Anyone setting compensation for expat staff, aid workers, or business travelers in these cities should recognize that “moderate local prices” doesn’t mean affordability for the people who actually live there because local salaries aren’t providing the cushion that similar price levels would provide elsewhere.






Figure 3



The bigger picture
This analysis seems to suggest that it may be inaccurate to treat “big city” and “expensive city” as synonyms. They’re not the same axis at all. I’d argue that a better way to evaluate where money goes further (whether that is the result of relocation, international hiring, or just curiosity) is to look at purchasing power relative to cost, not cost in isolation. By that measure, some of the most attractive cities I found for stretching a dollar rarely make anyone’s “expensive city” headlines.
Full code, data, and README are available on GitHub: cost-of-living-scraper
